_comment: Central balance sheet for the campaign system. This file is the single
source of truth: PHP reads it directly for multiplayer, and
tools/build-campaign-config.mjs generates js/data/actions.js from it for
solo play. Change a number here and both sides change together.
All money is in rupees. Support effects are percentage points.
Outcome weights are relative and need not sum to 100.
The actions below are fictional game mechanics. The 'risky' ones abstract
questionable political behaviour into a cost, a dice roll and a
consequence - they describe no real-world method and never explain how
anything would be done.

heat._consequenceComment: Chance of a consequence firing after an action = heat/100 * chanceFactor, floored below minHeat.
heat._coolComment: Heat cools slightly at each round end. Without it heat only ever climbs, so a single risky round would mark a player for the rest of the campaign and the risk system becomes a one-way door rather than a dial.

_comment: The sitting MLA's party starts ahead in their own seat. How far ahead is
rolled per seat from the game seed, so the map is not uniform and players
cannot assume every incumbent is equally hard to shift.
These numbers are a balance between two requirements that pull against each
other. Incumbency has to be a real advantage, or the verified MLA data is
decoration; but the real result must not simply replay, or the game is over
before anyone campaigns. partySwingSpread is what buys the second: each game
rolls one swing per party across every seat, so some open with a dominant
incumbent bloc and others with a genuine four-way fight.
As tuned (measure with: npm run measure:board, 60 games):
incumbents hold their own seat in 74 of 117 on average, range 22-110
the largest bloc opens on 76 on average, range 44-113
the incumbent party leads the board in roughly two games in three
After four players campaign, about a quarter of elections end hung.
othersHandicap keeps the unplayable Others bucket where it belongs: it holds
a couple of real seats and can win a handful, but it never gets a statewide
swing and never sweeps.
Advantage, swing and spread are all in percentage points of support.
Election day. Each seat is decided on its support plus a little noise, so
a narrow lead is not a guarantee and a close race can go either way.
seatNoise is in percentage points.
Post-election government formation. Version 1 allows two human players in
a coalition; the structure allows more later.
A proposal must be accepted by the other player, and either side can walk
away, in which case the talks fail and another pairing can be tried.

_comment: A fictional oversight mechanic layered on Political Heat.
Players may report a rival once each. Reports do not equal guilt: the
outcome is rolled against a hidden evidence score, so an innocent player
can be cleared even with three reports, and ganging up does not reliably
remove anyone.
Evidence is never shown to players. Weights are shifted by evidenceBias:
positive means more likely when evidence is high, negative means less.

evidence._comment: All contributions are capped so no single factor decides it.

_comment: Fifteen rounds of sixty seconds, with a short results break between them.
The clock is authoritative on the server: roundStartedAt is a server
timestamp and every response carries the server time, so clients compute the
remaining seconds from that rather than from their own clock. A refresh
therefore picks the round up where it stands.
Rounds advance lazily: whichever request arrives first after the clock runs
out processes the round end, under the same lock as everything else. With
clients polling every 2.5s a round turns over within a couple of seconds of
expiry, and nothing depends on a cron job the host may not have.
graceSeconds forgives an action that was in flight as the clock expired, so
a player who clicks on 00:00 is not punished for their latency.
actionsPerRound is what stops money deciding the game on its own. Without
it, a round rewards whoever clicks fastest, and a large purse converts
straight into support at the speed of the mouse. Three moves a round means
forty-five moves a campaign for everybody, so the question stops being how
much you can spend and becomes which three seats are worth it this minute.
intermissionSeconds is the results break. Play is locked while it runs, so
the scoreboard is not competing with the next round for the same seconds —
reading what just happened is part of the game, not a tax on it.
Cash and debt are tracked separately and cash may never go negative.
Loans are the interesting decision: money now against a bill two rounds
later, at a rate that hurts. Borrowing in round 13 or later is refused
because the bill would land after the campaign has closed, which would make
late borrowing free.
Defaulting is deliberately worse than the money involved: heat, a campaign
restriction and lost support. Otherwise the right play would always be to
borrow the maximum in the last rounds and never repay.

default.text: You could not repay. Word of the default is all over the campaign.

_comment: Two ways to raise money mid-campaign, with opposite characters.
A grant application is honest and unreliable: it costs a real amount of
work, usually returns less than it cost on its own, and carries no heat.
It is worth doing because the development spending also moves support.
Underground funding is the mirror image: it can pay several times over, but
it is the fastest way to raise heat in the game and can be taken away again
by an investigation. Both are fictional game mechanics; neither describes
any real-world method.

_reachComment: Why dearer actions reach further rather than simply hitting harder.
Every seat is normalised to 100 across five parties, so a large gain in
one seat is compressed on the way in: +4 raw lands as roughly +3, while
+2 raw lands as roughly +1.9. Raw support therefore has sharply
diminishing returns, and an action costing two and a half times as much
bought barely a tenth more effect. With three moves a round, that made
money almost irrelevant — the opposite of the intended balance, and
measurably worse than not spending at all once interest was counted.
Reach fixes it in the direction the subject suggests anyway. A doorstep
campaign moves one constituency. Media coverage and a statewide push are
seen in several. The extra seats take a fraction of the effect, so
spending more genuinely buys more — but it buys breadth, not certainty,
and choosing the right seat to aim at still matters more than the size of
the cheque. Bad outcomes spread the same way: a media campaign that goes

_comment: Thresholds for the round-results screen. All display, no rules.
closeRaceSeats decides when the top two are worth calling a close race.
Set it too high and every round looks like a photo finish, which stops
meaning anything; too low and genuinely tight elections pass unremarked.
maxSeatChangesShown caps the list of constituencies that changed hands.
Early rounds can flip forty seats at once, and a wall of them is worse
than a count — the rest are summarised as a total.
Opponents for the parties nobody is playing, so the scoreboard always has
four competitors and a solo game is still an election.
The AI plays by exactly the same rules as a human: the same actions, the
same costs, the same weighted outcomes, the same heat, the same three
moves a round, the same consequences when it runs hot. It has no extra
information and no extra money. What differs between the profiles is
temperament — how much risk it will take and how tightly it targets — so
the three opponents in a solo game do not all play the same way.
Names are drawn at random per game from the pools below. They are ordinary
Punjabi given names and surnames combined freely; any resemblance to a
particular living politician would be coincidence, and none of the pools
is built from real officeholders.

_menuComment: Which menu each action appears under.
The four safe strategies and the last-minute push are ordinary
campaigning. The rest are the high-risk ones, and they sit together under
their own heading so a player can see at a glance that everything on that
screen carries a real chance of going wrong.
This lives in the config rather than the interface so adding an action
puts it in the right place without anyone editing a screen.

_comment: How much to put behind a move is now the player's decision, not a fixed
price. Each action has a base cost; spending more or less than it scales
what the move achieves.
The curve is a square root, and that choice carries the whole balance of
the feature. Spending four times the base cost buys twice the effect, not
four times it — so for a fixed budget the most efficient play is to spread
money evenly across every move you have, never to dump it into a few.
That is exactly the behaviour we want: money should buy a real advantage
without letting a rich campaign simply purchase the election in three
expensive gestures.
The clamps stop both ends running away. Below minScale a token amount
would otherwise look like a bargain, since a move costs one of the three
a round whatever is spent; above maxScale a single move could swing a seat
outright.
Heat scales with the money too. Putting four times the money behind a
risky move is four times as visible, and it should be.
